frameworks.name: $500K Employee Roadmap
frameworks.definition: A structured path for an employee to increase compensation from $50K to $500K by moving to a larger company, positioning themselves near revenue generation, taking on entrepreneurial risk, and negotiating for a percentage of value created.

frameworks.name: Value-to-Compensation Negotiation
frameworks.definition: A framework for employees to articulate measurable business impact they create, propose performance-based upside, and negotiate for a share of that created value.

frameworks.name: Internal Revenue Attribution
frameworks.definition: The discipline of mapping every role's contribution to business revenue generation, from direct (sales) to indirect (customer success, finance, legal), enabling conversations about compensation alignment.

claims.text: To earn $500K annually as an employee, you must work at a company generating at least $10-20M in annual revenue, unless you are the CEO. Smaller companies lack sufficient profit to pay that compensation level.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: employee position
not CEO
salary-based compensation structure
claims.mechanism: Revenue size determines total profit pool available for employee compensation; a $500K company cannot pay $500K salaries to multiple employees.
bounded_by: Does not apply to CEO roles with bonus/equity
Does not apply to equity-based compensation models

claims.text: Employees increase earning potential by positioning themselves as close to revenue generation as possible, similar to how entrepreneurs tie compensation to business outcomes. The foundational mindset is thinking of yourself as a vendor or service provider to the business, not an employee.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: salaried employee position
company willing to negotiate performance-based pay
measurable business impact possible
claims.mechanism: When an employee adopts an entrepreneurial vendor mindset and can articulate a clear revenue impact, they shift from fixed-salary thinking to value-created thinking. This reframing unlocks negotiation leverage for performance-based upside similar to entrepreneur-business relationships.
bounded_by: Does not apply in companies with rigid salary bands that reject performance-based negotiation
Does not apply in commoditized roles without clear revenue attribution

claims.text: An employee proposing a quantified business improvement should ask: 'If I generate an additional $5M in revenue for the company, will you give me 10% of that $5M as additional compensation?' Most business-savvy owners will agree to this trade, though the employee receives a discount compared to what an external entrepreneur would capture.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: employee can articulate specific, measurable business outcome
outcome is quantifiable in revenue terms
company owner is business-minded
claims.mechanism: Specificity and quantification shift the conversation from negotiation (where power dynamics favor the employer) to transaction (where the employee demonstrates value creation). The 10% target acknowledges that employees always receive a discount relative to full business ownership but retain certainty and stability advantages.
bounded_by: Assumes business owner views employee contributions as revenue-generating; does not apply to cost-center roles
Assumes employee can credibly deliver on the outcome promise

claims.text: If an employee in customer success proposes cutting churn from 10% to 5%, they should frame it as an owned outcome: 'If I can reduce churn to 5%, will you increase my compensation?' The upside is capped or absent if the company refuses this performance-based model.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: role has measurable second-order impact on revenue (churn reduction)
employee willing to own outcome accountability
company has historical churn baseline to measure against
claims.mechanism: Second-order revenue impacts (churn, customer success, retention) are less obviously tied to business value than first-order ones (direct sales). Explicitly owning the outcome and proposing performance-based compensation reframes the role from cost-center to revenue-center.
bounded_by: Does not apply in customer success roles where pricing/packaging makes churn improvement impossible
Does not apply if company has no mechanism to pass savings/revenue gains back to employees

claims.text: When proposing performance-based compensation, the employee should control as much of the outcome and inputs (time, money, resources) as possible. The more of the outcome the employee owns, the more upside they can unlock.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: employee-employer relationship where negotiation is possible
outcome is partially controllable by the employee
claims.mechanism: Ownership of inputs (time, budget) and outcomes reduces the employer's perception of risk and increases the employer's willingness to share upside. An employee who says 'I'll take on this risk and fund it' is more credible than one asking for resources and upside simultaneously.
bounded_by: Does not apply in roles with shared accountability (matrix organizations, cross-functional teams)
Does not apply if company policy prohibits individual outcome ownership

claims.text: Many companies will refuse to negotiate performance-based compensation or cap upside for employees. In this case, the employee has reached a genuine compensation ceiling and should leave to find a company open to the value-sharing model.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: employee has proposed performance-based model
company explicitly or implicitly rejected it
employee has higher-leverage opportunities available
claims.mechanism: Refusing employee value-sharing proposals is economically irrational for business owners (leaving money on the table), so the mismatch signals a fundamental misalignment in compensation philosophy. Staying in such a company is a capped-upside trap.
bounded_by: Does not apply if the employee lacks concrete proposals or track record
Does not apply if the company is genuinely capital-constrained (startup, new business)

claims.text: Every employee role—sales, customer service, finance, legal—should be able to articulate clearly how their work makes the company money. If an employee cannot explain this linkage, the role lacks revenue attribution and negotiating for upside becomes difficult.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: employee seeks to negotiate performance-based compensation
role has some measurable or second-order business impact
claims.mechanism: Business owners who understand the revenue impact of every role are more willing to share upside because they can quantify the value. Employees who can articulate this linkage are credible negotiators. Inability to articulate it signals either a low-value role or an employee who lacks business acumen.
bounded_by: Does not apply to pure support roles (e.g., facilities, HR administration) with no revenue linkage
Does not apply in companies where financial information is not shared with employees

claims.text: An employee who believes they can deliver a specific outcome should ask: 'What resources (money, time) are you asking me to put into this? How much capital do I have to deploy?' The employee's answer determines how much upside they can claim.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: employee proposing a performance-based deal
outcome requires resource deployment
claims.mechanism: Employees who assume capital risk (their own time, budget, or resources) can claim a larger share of upside because they are reducing the employer's risk. An employee saying 'I'll fund this myself and pocket the upside if I succeed' is more credible than one asking for resources and upside simultaneously.
bounded_by: Does not apply if company policy prohibits employee capital deployment
Does not apply if the required capital is so large that the employee cannot afford it

examples.text: A customer service representative who is stuck in a fixed-salary role at a company that refuses performance-based compensation has hit a genuine earnings ceiling. No amount of effort or skill improvement will increase compensation above the salary band. The employee's only path to $500K is to leave and find a larger company open to value-sharing, or to start a business.

A finance person at a large company might articulate: 'I manage cash flow and accounts receivable. If I optimize our collection cycle by 10 days, we free up $500K in working capital that can be reinvested. If I can deliver that, would you increase my compensation by $50K?' This explicit linkage transforms a 'cost-center' role into a 'revenue-center' proposal because the freed capital has measurable business value.

A sales rep at a low-compensation company might propose: 'I can generate $5M in additional revenue. I want 10% of that as additional compensation, which is $500K. I will also fund the marketing and prospecting costs myself using my own capital. Are you open to that?' This proposal owns both the outcome (revenue generation) and the resource deployment (marketing budget), making it credible.

practices.text: As an employee seeking higher compensation, walk around your company and ask colleagues: 'How do you make us money?' Listen to their answers. If they cannot articulate a clear business impact, they are likely in a capped-upside role.

Reframe your identity from 'employee' to 'internal vendor or service provider to the business.' Ask yourself: 'In what way does what I do generate revenue for this company?' If you cannot answer clearly, invest in building a skill that does.

Before accepting or negotiating a role at a company, research their size and revenue. If you want to earn $500K and the company is $100M in revenue, verify that the company has historically paid $500K+ to non-CEO employees. If not, you have set an unrealistic ceiling.

When proposing performance-based compensation, be specific about the outcome (e.g., 'reduce churn from 10% to 5%'), the resources you need, and the resources you will own. The more you own, the larger your claim on upside.
